source_title: Low-Temperature Specific Heats of Zr-Ti, Zr-Hf, and Zr-Sc Alloys
note: Alloy Zr0.75Sc0.25, in the continuous hcp Zr-Sc solid solution. Betterton & Scarbrough (Phys. Rev. 168, 715, 1968) measured specific heats of hexagonal Zr-Sc alloys from 1.1 to 4.2 K and found no superconductivity anywhere in the Zr-Sc system. They also say Sc depresses superconductivity in the Zr-rich region, where pure Zr has Tc of about 0.55 K. Jensen & Maita (Phys. Rev. 149, 409, 1966) found that the Sc-Zr alloys with the largest electronic specific heat (the Sc-rich end) do not superconduct down to 0.03 K. Two caveats. I saw only the abstracts, because APS, ADS, Scilit and NIST were unreachable from this session, so I could not confirm that an alloy within about 2 at.% of 25 at.% Sc was in either series. A sub-kelvin Tc below 0.55 K at this composition in the 1966 dilution-refrigerator data cannot be ruled out. Hence low confidence.

Alloy Ag0.60Cd0.40, at the Cd-rich limit of the fcc alpha solid solution (about 40-42 at.% Cd at room temperature). I found no superconductivity report for any Ag-Cd alloy. Pure Ag is not a superconductor and pure Cd has Tc of about 0.52 K. Specific heats of alpha-phase AgCd alloys were measured from 1 to 4 K (Proc. R. Soc. A 301, 261, 1967, DOI 10.1098/rspa.1967.0207; Montgomery & Pells, Proc. Phys. Soc. 78, 622, 1961). The available abstracts describe only dilute Cd additions, and I could not confirm that any alloy near 40 at.% Cd was measured. No low-temperature transport or susceptibility data was found near this composition.

source_title: Incipient superconductivity in TaB2
note: HfB2 is an AlB2-type metal and essentially a Pauli paramagnet. Leyarovska & Leyarovski (J. Less-Common Met. 67, 249, 1979) found no superconductivity in transition-metal diborides, HfB2 included, down to 0.42 K; only NbB2 superconducted (0.62 K). Kaczorowski et al. (2001) re-measured HfB2 and found it not superconducting above 1.7 K. Barbero et al. (arXiv:1703.03253, 2017) state that pure HfB2 shows no superconductivity above 1 K and give a flat R(T) from 2 K. Superconductivity appears only on V doping: Hf0.97V0.03B2 has Tc = 7.31 K, which is the doped exception.

Ru2P is orthorhombic Pnma, anti-PbCl2/Co2Si type (Materials Project PRu2). I found no report of a superconducting transition, low-T resistivity, susceptibility or heat capacity for stoichiometric Ru2P. An arXiv full-text search returned no Ru2P papers, and in RuP studies Ru2P appears only as an impurity phase. Related compounds that do superconduct are different phases: Rh-doped RuP (Ru1-xRhxP, Tc up to about 3.7 K), LaRu2P2 (about 4 K), ZrRuP (about 13 K), and Rh2P (reported 1.3 K). The 1965 survey of superconducting transition-metal phosphides by Blaugher, Hulm & Yocom (J. Phys. Chem. Solids 26, 2037) could not be read here, so I could not check whether Ru2P was tested in it.

source_title: Thermal conductivity of strong coupling V1-xTix superconductors in the Mott-Ioffe-Regel limit
note: Alloy V0.88Ti0.12, a bcc beta solid solution. Arc-melted polycrystalline V1-xTix with x = 0.1 (V0.90Ti0.10, 2 at.% from the target) is a bulk superconductor with TC = 6.4 K. TC was taken from heat capacity, and thermal conductivity was measured from 2 to 8 K. Pure V has TC = 5.4 K, and in this series TC rises with Ti content, peaking near 30-40 at.% Ti. The value 6.4 K is for x = 0.10; the TC at x = 0.12 itself was not tabulated, but should be close or slightly higher.
second_reader_reason: I checked this against the full text of arXiv:1810.02083v1. arxiv.org itself could not be reached from this session. The paper covers bulk arc-melted polycrystalline bcc beta-V1−xTix alloys at ambient pressure. The x = 0.10 alloy (V0.90Ti0.10, 2 at.% from the target V0.88Ti0.12) has TC = 6.4 K, from heat capacity, and the thermal conductivity drops in the superconducting state between 2 and 8 K. This fits the 2 at.% alloy rule. Supporting data: the SuperCon compilation (Stanev 2018, in the local 3DSC repo) lists Ti0.106V0.894 at 6.86 K, Ti0.1V0.9 at 5.89 K and Ti0.2V0.8 at 7.305 K. Caveat a sceptic should note: the same compilation lists Ti0.12V0.88 with Tc = 0, its code for a non-superconductor. That entry disagrees with every neighbouring composition, I could not trace its primary source, and it is probably a record with no Tc entered. So the verdict stands, with the exact-composition Tc unconfirmed; 6.4 K is the value at x = 0.10.

note: Two searches found no paper reporting superconductivity, or a stated lowest measurement temperature, for La5Sn3. One search summary said a heavy-fermion study of Ce5Sn3 uses La5Sn3 as a non-magnetic resistivity reference, so transport data probably exist, but I could not open that paper or establish how low it was measured. A J. Phys. Colloq. 1978 record (doi 10.1051/jphyscol:19786392) came up as the top hit but its host was unreachable, so its content is unknown. source_title: Condensed Matter (MDPI) 7(1), 25 - pressure study of La(O,F)BiS2 / LaOBiS2 single crystals (exact title not retrieved)

The undoped compound is reported as an insulator/semiconductor (direct gap about 0.8-1.0 eV) with no superconductivity down to 0.2 K. Superconductivity appears only on electron doping: F for O gives Tc up to about 2.5 K at ambient pressure, and tetravalent Ti/Zr/Hf/Th for La gives Tc up to 2.85 K (arXiv:1303.6216, which calls the parent a 'bad metal' rather than an insulator). tc_k is null because the stoichiometric compound has no Tc. The quote is from a search-result excerpt; mdpi.com and arxiv.org were unreachable from this session, so the full text and the exact article title were not checked.
second_reader_reason: I agree with the verdict but could not verify the citation. The cited MDPI paper (Condensed Matter 7(1), 25) and its quote 'no superconductivity down to 0.2 K' could not be opened: mdpi.com, arxiv.org and doi.org are blocked in this session and the web-search budget was used up. The 2.85 K for La0.85Th0.15OBiS2 matches the first pass's 1303.6216 claim. Under the definitions this is superconductivity only after doping, so the verdict stands. The 0.2 K lowest temperature and the MDPI source are unconfirmed.

note: Two searches found no report of a CdBi compound or of low-temperature measurements on a 50:50 Cd-Bi alloy. From memory, not confirmed by a source in this session: Cd-Bi is a simple eutectic system with no equilibrium intermediate compound at ambient pressure, so this composition would be a two-phase mixture of the elements; pure Cd superconducts near 0.5 K. The searches only returned elemental Bi (about 0.53 mK at ambient pressure; Bi-II 3.9 K and Bi-III 7 K under pressure) and unrelated bismuthides. source_title: Superconductivity in the Narrow-Gap Semiconductor CsBi4Te6
note: Cs(Bi2Te3)2 is CsBi4Te6, a narrow-gap semiconductor best known as a low-temperature thermoelectric. Superconductivity near 4.4 K is reported only for p-type (hole-doped) samples; the same paper states that the stoichiometric compound is not a superconductor. Related doped variants also superconduct: CsPbxBi4-xTe6 (Tc up to 3.1 K, orthorhombic phase) and Na/K-doped CsBi4Te6 (up to 5.07 K). tc_k is null because the stoichiometric compound has no Tc. The lowest temperature of the measurement on the stoichiometric sample was not stated in the abstract.
second_reader_reason: I agree with the verdict but could not open the cited JACS paper (doi 10.1021/ja407530u). pubs.acs.org and doi.org are blocked and the web-search budget was used up, so the quoted abstract sentences were not checked. Independent support comes from the SuperCon compilation in the local 3DSC repo. Stoichiometric CsBi4Te6 is listed with Tc = 0 (non-superconductor). The superconducting entries are off-stoichiometric Cs0.96Bi4Te6 and CsBi4.1Te5.9, both at 4.4 K, and Pb-substituted CsPbxBi4-xTe6 at 2.7-2.9 K. This matches the first pass exactly: 4.4 K only in p-type, off-stoichiometric samples, and the stoichiometric compound does not superconduct. The compound is a narrow-gap semiconductor, but superconductivity is reported in off-stoichiometric and doped samples, so under the definitions the right class is superconductor_only_pressure_doping_or_film. No lowest temperature for the stoichiometric sample was confirmed.

source_title: Large magnetoresistance and weak-antilocalization in the nodal-line semimetal VP2
note: VP2 single crystals are described as a type-II nodal-line semimetal. Resistivity was measured and fitted over 2-80 K, showing a Kondo upturn attributed to about 2.24% V4+ magnetic impurities, plus large non-saturating magnetoresistance and weak antilocalization. No superconducting transition is mentioned and no magnetic order is reported. No other paper reporting superconductivity in VP2 was found. The 2 K figure comes from a search-result excerpt of the paper and a review page; arxiv.org was unreachable from this session, so the full text was not opened.

Th0.9Er0.1 alloy. I found no low-temperature transport, susceptibility or heat-capacity data at or near 10 at.% Er in Th. Nearby data: pure Th superconducts at about 1.37-1.38 K, and magnetic rare earths suppress this very quickly. A CNEA report (citing Finnemore, Johnson and Ostenson, Phys. Rev. 137, 1550 (1965)) gives Tc of about 0.96 K for Th + 0.15 at.% Gd and about 0.65 K for Th + 0.25 at.% Gd. Tc measurements of Th with ppm-level Er exist (Davidov et al. cite them in an ESR study of 40-3250 ppm Gd, Er and Dy in Th). By Abrikosov-Gor'kov pair breaking, 10 at.% Er would be expected to destroy superconductivity, but that is an inference, not a measurement. The magnetic papers by Koehler et al. (J. Appl. Phys. 38, 1384 (1967), Th-Ho/Er alloys) and Child, Koehler and Millhouse (J. Appl. Phys. 39, 1329 (1968), fcc RE-Th alloys at roughly 50 at.% Th or more, neutron data to 1.3 K) appear to cover far more Er-rich compositions. Their full texts could not be read, so I could not tell whether a 10 at.% Er alloy was measured.

Ag0.85In0.15 (about 15.8 wt.% In) lies inside the fcc alpha solid solution of Ag-In (solubility limit about 20 wt.% In), so it is a single-phase fcc alloy. I found no superconductivity measurement tied to this composition. Closest leads: (1) Phys. Rev. B 1, 3002 (1970), 'Superconductivity in Noble-Metal-Rich Hexagonal Close-Packed Phases'. Its abstract says fcc solid solutions of the noble metals with Zn, Cd, Al and In 'remained normal down to 0.014 K', while hcp phases (including ones with In) superconduct at 0.019-0.61 K. The abstract does not say which noble metal or which composition was used for the In alloy, and the full text was unreachable, so I cannot confirm that Ag-15In was measured. If it was, the verdict would become measured_no_superconductivity with a lowest temperature of 0.014 K. (2) Electronic specific heat of alpha-phase Ag-In alloys was measured in the liquid-helium range (Phys. Rev. B 5, 2057 (1972)); compositions not seen. (3) Hoyt and Mota (Solid State Commun. 18, 139 (1976); 20, 1025 (1976)) found mK superconductivity in some alpha-phase noble-metal alloys (Cu-Si, Cu-Ge, Ag-Ge, Ag-Al, Au-Ge, Au-Zn), but Ag-In is not among the systems listed. Pure Ag is not a superconductor.

Mo0.85Ni0.15. I found no low-temperature transport, susceptibility or heat-capacity data for Mo-rich Mo-Ni alloys near this composition, whether bulk, splat-quenched, amorphous or film. From memory of the phase diagram (not verified in a source here): Ni dissolves only about 1-2 at.% in bcc Mo, so at equilibrium Mo85Ni15 should be a two-phase mixture of Mo(Ni) and the delta-NiMo intermetallic. Nearby facts: pure Mo superconducts at about 0.92 K. Ni-rich Ni1-xMox (x = 0.06-0.14) is a paramagnet near a ferromagnetic quantum critical point (arXiv:2503.00484), a clearly different composition. Searches turned up Mo-Re, Mo-Nb, Mo-N and Mo-Ru-P superconductors, but nothing on Mo-Ni.

source_title: Tuning electronic correlations in the Kagome metals RT3B2
note: YCo3B2 has the hexagonal CeCo3B2-type structure (P6/mmm) with a Co kagome lattice. It is a Pauli paramagnet: J. Appl. Phys. (1994), 'Magnetic susceptibility of RCo3B2 (R=Y, Sm, Gd, and Dy)', reports Pauli paramagnetism down to 5 K, and band calculations agree. Its low-temperature resistivity goes as T^2, attributed to spin fluctuations (Kowalczyk et al., Acta Phys. Pol. A 97, 2000). It does not order magnetically. The 2025 arXiv study measured it alongside superconducting LuOs3B2 and found no superconductivity down to 1.8 K. Isostructural Ru/Os analogues (e.g. LuOs3B2, YRu3B2) do superconduct; the Co compound does not.

source_title: Superconductivity in the Alloy System Cadmium-Mercury and the Effect of Ordering upon Superconductivity
note: Hg0.95Cd0.05. Claeson, Luo and Merriam (Phys. Rev. 141, 412 (1966)) measured Tc of Cd-Hg alloys across the whole composition range. Their phase boundaries matter here: Cd dissolves in solid Hg only up to 1.5 +/- 0.25 at.% at 193 K, and the intermediate omega phase begins at 88 +/- 1 at.% Hg. So a 5 at.% Cd alloy is a two-phase mixture of Hg(Cd) solid solution and omega phase, not a single solid solution. Both neighbouring phases fall in the range the paper reports as superconducting. A 2015 review (Webb et al., arXiv:1502.04724) also notes that Hg-Cd alloys were found superconducting soon after 1911. I could not read the numerical Tc for about 5 at.% Cd: the full text was unreachable from this session. I therefore leave tc_k empty and do not guess it; physically it should be close to Hg's 4.15 K. A 1932 Leiden paper by de Haas and de Boer reports Hg-lattice alloys with 30-50 at.% Cd, but its scanned values could not be checked. The verdict rests on the full-range statement, not on a measurement confirmed at exactly 5 at.% Cd, which is why confidence is not high.
second_reader_reason: The first-pass claim fails. Under the definitions, superconductor_ambient needs a Tc and a source saying this composition superconducts. The first pass gave no Tc, and its quote ('Tc of Cd-Hg alloys covering the complete composition range have been determined') does not say that Hg0.95Cd0.05 superconducts. I could not open Claeson, Luo and Merriam, Phys. Rev. 141, 412 (1966): journals.aps.org and doi.org are blocked and the web-search budget was used up, so neither its abstract nor any Tc near 5 at.% Cd was checked. The SuperCon compilation in the local 3DSC repo points the other way: it lists Cd0.05Hg0.95 and Cd0.1Hg0.9 with Tc = 0, its code for non-superconductors. It also lists Cd0.3Hg0.7 at 1.7 K, CdHg at 1.31 K and pure Hg at 4.14 K. That zero is odd, because the first pass's own phase-boundary argument implies a two-phase Hg(Cd) + omega mixture that should superconduct near the Hg Tc. The database gives no lowest temperature or primary reference, so measured_no_superconductivity cannot be given either. With no confirmed low-temperature measurement at about 5 at.% Cd, the honest verdict is no_low_temperature_data_found. Nearby compositions: pure Hg is 4.15 K, Hg-richer omega/CdHg-type compositions are about 1.3-1.7 K, and Cd-rich alloys are about 0.5 K.

source_title: Heavy-electron behavior in single-crystal YbNi2B2C (Yatskar, Budraa, Beyermann, Canfield, Bud'ko, Phys. Rev. B 54, R3772)
note: Single crystals are a nonmagnetic Kondo-lattice heavy fermion (gamma about 530 mJ/mol K^2, T_K about 10 K). They show no magnetic order and no superconductivity, unlike the superconducting LuNi2B2C and YNi2B2C and the magnetic RNi2B2C members. Yatskar et al. measured susceptibility, specific heat and resistivity down to 0.34 K. Bud'ko/Avila/Canfield (arXiv cond-mat/0410090) state there is no superconductivity or long-range magnetic order above 0.03 K, citing earlier work. Dhar et al. (Solid State Commun. 98, 985, 1996) also found no superconductivity down to 2 K in polycrystals. A 2019 APS abstract reports neither superconductivity nor magnetism at ambient pressure down to 50 mK, but I could not open it. I give 0.34 K because I could check that value directly.

source_title: Nodeless superconductivity in the cage-type superconductor Sc5Ru6Sn18 with preserved time-reversal symmetry (context only; not this compound)
note: I found no report of a Lu-Ru-Sn phase called Lu4Ru6Sn19 (also searched Lu5Ru6Sn18, Lu5-xRu6Sn18+x and the Lu-Ru-Sn phase diagram). The formula matches x = 1 of the Remeika-type Lu5-xT6Sn18+x family (Tb5Rh6Sn18 type, with the mixed R/Sn site fully Sn). Related phases superconduct: Lu5Rh6Sn18 at Tc about 4 K and Sc5Ru6Sn18 at Tc about 3.5 K. The Sc5Ru6Sn18 paper says the superconductivity of the Ru stannides R5Ru6Sn18 is 'largely unexplored'. A 2026 preprint (arXiv 2602.22448) studies R5M6Sn18 and R3M4Sn13 with R = Y, La, Lu and M = Co, Rh, Ru, but the full text has no Lu-Ru-Sn data. The source given is for the closest relative only, not this compound.

source_title: Superconductivity, Susceptibility, and Specific Heat in the Noble Transition Elements and Alloys. I. Experimental Results (Andres & Jensen) - context only
note: This is the fcc alloy Ir0.7Rh0.3. Pure Ir superconducts at about 0.11-0.14 K and pure Rh at about 325 microkelvin. Andres & Jensen (Phys. Rev. 165, 533, 1968) measured Tc and susceptibility of fcc Ir alloys with Ru, Rh, Pd, Re, Os and Pt, mostly on the Ir-rich side, down to 0.015 K. I could not get their Ir-Rh value at or near 30 at.% Rh, so I cannot say whether this alloy superconducts above 0.015 K. A Phys. Lett. A paper, 'Toward the superconductivity of rhodium', measured Rh-Ir and Rh-Os alloys on the Rh-rich side, which is a much different composition. Expect Tc somewhere between the Ir and Rh values or below 0.015 K, but this is not verified. The source given is for context only.

I found no experimental report of a Mo5O2 (Mo0.714O0.286) phase. Searches for synthesis, structure, transport or superconductivity found only formula-calculator pages. The known binary Mo oxides are MoO2, Mo4O11, Mo8O23, Mo17O47 and MoO3, all more oxygen-rich than this. Nearby claims are at clearly different compositions: a Tc of about 12 K was attributed to an MoO2-delta impurity phase (Parker et al., Phys. Rev. B 90, 054505, 2014), and in sputtered Mo-based films added oxygen lowers Tc. This is most likely a computed or hypothetical database entry.

source_title: The Superconductivity of Some Intermetallic Compounds (Blaugher, Taylor, Hulm, IBM J. Res. Dev. 6, 116) - context only; W-Re data at 10 at.% not retrieved
note: This is the bcc solid solution W0.9Re0.1. Blaugher, Taylor & Hulm (IBM J. Res. Dev. 6, 116, 1962) tested Re-W down to 1 K and, as far as search snippets show, report a rapid rise of Tc in the bcc W-rich region. I could not get the paper's Tc-versus-composition figure, so I have no value at 10 at.% Re. Nearby compositions: pure W has Tc about 0.012 K. A D-Wave patent family (JP5296189B2) says W-3%Re superconducts only below 1 K. The same patents (e.g. US9779360), citing Blaugher et al., describe W-10%Re to W-30%Re as having Tc above the temperatures reachable with liquid helium; this is a secondary, non-peer-reviewed reading. The bcc branch peaks at about 5 K near the Re solubility limit (Roberts 1976, cited in Shang et al., arXiv 2105.11600). CVD alloys (3.5-95 at.% Re, Easton et al., Phil. Mag. 30, 1117, 1974) have higher Tc than arc-melted ones. The alloy is probably superconducting at roughly 1 K or above, but I found no measured Tc at this composition, so I did not label it a superconductor. The source given is for context only.

source_title: Robust Superconductivity and High Upper Critical Fields in Epitaxial cubic W2N Thin Films
note: The only clear experimental superconductivity in stoichiometric W2N is in thin films: 270 nm epitaxial cubic W2N films sputtered on Al2O3 and MgO have Tc about 5 K and Hc2 about 8.5 T (preprint, 2025). The 'bulk nature' claim in that paper is a diamagnetic signal from the film, not a measurement on bulk material. Older work on reactively sputtered W-N films found Tc up to 4.85 K, but those films were multiphase (beta-W plus W2N). Liang et al., Adv. Funct. Mater. 34, 2313819 (2024), a diamond-anvil-cell study of W2N3 and W3N5, says W2N 'shows a Tc of 1.3 K at ambient conditions'. I could not find the primary data behind that 1.3 K figure or tell whether it was measured on bulk material, so I did not count it as a bulk ambient report. If it is confirmed as bulk, the verdict would become superconductor_ambient with Tc about 1.3 K. Bulk stoichiometric cubic beta-W2N is metastable and usually nitrogen-deficient. The other superconducting W-N compounds (W2N3, W3N5) are different phases, made at high pressure. tc_k is the film value. The cubic film phase may differ from the Materials Project W2N structure.
second_reader_reason: I opened the arXiv abstract and full PDF myself. The paper exists and matches what the first pass said. The films are single-phase, epitaxial, cubic NaCl-type W2N with half the nitrogen sites filled, about 270 nm thick. Tc is about 5.0 K on Al2O3 and 5.06 K on MgO, with a diamagnetic transition near 5 K. The authors call this 'bulk nature', but all measurements are on films. The paper calls itself 'the first comprehensive experimental investigation of superconductivity in stoichiometric W2N'. It says earlier W-N work was on multiphase sputtered films (W, beta-W and W2N inclusions), so the intrinsic properties 'remained ambiguous'. The only ambient-pressure figure for non-film material is the passing mention of 'near 1.3 K', cited to Liang et al. 2024, which is a high-pressure synthesis paper. I could not open Liang et al.: onlinelibrary.wiley.com and api.crossref.org are blocked from this session, and the web-search budget for this turn was used up. So the primary source behind 1.3 K, and whether it was bulk, remain unknown. Bulk ambient superconductivity of W2N is not established, and the only confirmed superconductivity is in films. tc_k is the film value. Caveat: the film phase is cubic (rocksalt-derived, PDF 00-025-1257), which may not be the Materials Project W2N structure.

source_title: Superconducting properties of Ti-Nb-Hf alloys
note: The composition is Ti0.64Nb0.32Hf0.04, a Hf-modified Ti-rich bcc Nb-Ti alloy close to commercial Nb-Ti wire compositions. Wada, Tachikawa and Kato (IEEE Trans. Magn. 17, 61, 1981) measured Tc and Hc2 on 42 Ti-Nb-Hf alloys spanning 25-65 at% Nb and 0-15 at% Hf (balance Ti), a range that includes this composition. All were superconducting, with Tc depending on Hf content and aging. They report Ti-40Nb-3Hf has Tc about 0.3 K above Ti-40Nb, with Hc2(4.2 K) = 11.7 T. The same group made multifilamentary wire from Ti-61.7 at%Ti-35.3Nb-3Hf (about 3 at% from this composition). I could not reach the full composition table, so I cannot give a measured Tc for this exact composition, and I left tc_k null rather than estimate it. From binary Nb-Ti data it is likely about 8-10 K, but that is an expectation, not a sourced value. Being within 2 at% of a measured alloy is likely but not confirmed.
second_reader_reason: Hf(Ti2Nb)8 is HfTi16Nb8, which is Ti0.64Nb0.32Hf0.04. The first pass gave superconductor_ambient but with no Tc, and it said itself that it could not find a measurement at or within 2 at% of this composition. I could not open the cited Wada/Tachikawa/Kato IEEE Trans. Magn. paper (host blocked). Publisher and DOI hosts other than arXiv were unreachable, and no further searches were allowed, so I found no other source. The abstract as quoted by the first pass gives a composition range (25-65 at% Nb, 0-15 at% Hf) that includes this alloy. Covering a range is not a measurement at this composition, though, and the one specific alloy quoted (Ti-40Nb-3Hf) is about 8 at% away in Nb. That is outside the 2 at% window. Under the alloy rule this is no_low_temperature_data_found, not superconductor_ambient. What nearby compositions do: Ti-rich bcc Ti-Nb and Ti-Nb-Hf alloys in this range are generally superconducting, with Tc of roughly 8-10 K from memory, and Ti-40Nb-3Hf is reported (per the quoted abstract, unverified by me) to superconduct about 0.3 K above Ti-40Nb. So the alloy is very likely a superconductor, but I could not confirm a sourced Tc for Ti-32Nb-4Hf. If the Wada et al. composition table can be opened and lists an alloy within about 2 at% (for example Ti-30/35Nb-3/5Hf), the verdict should become superconductor_ambient with that Tc.

note: The composition is Bi0.95Pb0.05. I found no low-temperature transport, susceptibility or heat-capacity data on bulk Bi-Pb alloys at or near 95 at% Bi. Nearby information: Pb dissolves only slightly in Bi, so bulk Bi0.95Pb0.05 at equilibrium should be mostly rhombohedral Bi plus a minor Pb-rich eutectic or epsilon (Pb7Bi3-type) phase. That phase superconducts at about 8.5-9 K (Pb0.64Bi0.36 Tc = 8.6 K, arXiv 2411.18315; Pb7Bi3-rich samples about 8.7-9 K, arXiv 2404.14773), so a filamentary or minority-phase transition near 8-9 K is plausible but has not been reported for this composition. Can. J. Phys. 43, 594 (1965) reports that Bi films and Bi films with small amounts of Pb are not superconducting above 1 K, but these are films with unspecified Pb content. Pure Bi superconducts only at about 0.53 mK. Metastable splat-quenched Bi-rich phases exist (e.g. near 89 at% Bi), but I found no Tc data for them.

source_title: Magnetic Structure of DyC2 (M. Atoji, J. Chem. Phys. 48, 3384)
note: DyC2 (tetragonal CaC2-type rare-earth dicarbide) orders antiferromagnetically at TN about 59 K, with a transverse, incommensurate spin-wave structure (moment wavelength about 1.3a), from neutron diffraction. A second weak-moment arrangement coexists below about 31 K. No superconductivity has been reported. Among RC2 compounds superconductivity is known only for non-magnetic ones such as YC2 and LaC2. The lowest measurement temperature is not given in the snippets I could access, so lowest_temperature_measured_k is null.

source_title: Low-Temperature Specific Heats of Zr-Ti, Zr-Hf, and Zr-Sc Alloys
note: The composition is Zr0.9Sc0.1, an hcp solid solution and a paramagnetic metal. The 1968 Phys. Rev. study measured the specific heat of hexagonal Zr-Sc alloys from 1.1 to 4.2 K and found no superconductivity anywhere in the Zr-Sc system. Its electronic specific-heat coefficient has a minimum near 10 at% Sc, so this composition is in the measured range. The 1.1 K floor is above the Tc of pure Zr (about 0.55-0.6 K), so the null result is expected. The authors note that Sc depresses Tc in the Zr-rich region. Jensen, Phys. Rev. 149, 409 (1966) measured Sc-Zr alloys down to 0.03 K: the alloys with the largest gamma (Sc-rich) were not superconducting, but I could not get his Tc values for Zr-rich compositions. A very low Tc (below about 0.5 K) at 10% Sc therefore cannot be ruled out. I worked from the abstract only, not the full text.

source_title: Kondo behavior and metamagnetic phase transition in a heavy fermion compound CeBi2 (Zhou et al., Phys. Rev. B 97, 195120)
note: CeBi2 is a Kondo-lattice heavy-fermion antiferromagnet with TN of about 3.3 K, a Sommerfeld coefficient above 200 mJ/mol K^2 and a metamagnetic transition in the ordered state. Resistance measured at ambient pressure down to 1.8 K shows no superconductivity. Above about 1.7 GPa, resistance drops that look like superconductivity appear in both CeBi2 and LaBi2. Specific heat under pressure shows no superconducting anomaly, however, so Xiang et al. (arXiv:1907.08645) conclude the superconductivity is not bulk and probably comes from traces of Bi flux. TN rises from 3.3 K to 4.4 K at 2.55 GPa. This is not a reported superconductor.

source_title: The ternary system cerium-palladium-silicon (Lipatov et al., J. Solid State Chem. 182, 2497) - phase identification only, no low-temperature data
note: Ce5(Si4Pd)2 is Ce5Pd2Si8, also written CePd0.4Si1.6 or Ce(Pd0.2Si0.8)2. Lipatov et al. (2009) mapped the Ce-Pd-Si phase diagram and reported Ce(PdxSi1-x)2 solid solutions of the AlB2-derivative (tau2) and alpha-ThSi2 (tau6) types, in which Pd and Si substitute randomly. This composition appears to fall in that region. I found no transport, susceptibility or heat-capacity data at or within about 2 at.% of this composition. Nearby compositions: Ce2PdSi3 (16.7 at.% Pd, about 3.4 at.% away) is an antiferromagnetic Kondo lattice with TN of about 3 K (Saha et al., PRB 62, 425, 2000). Pd-free CeSi2 is a nonmagnetic intermediate-valent compound. Si-deficient CeSi1.81 is ferromagnetic with TC = 9.5 K (PRB 73, 214413). No superconductivity is reported for any of them. The web-search budget ran out during this task, so the search was not exhaustive.

source_title: Electronic-structure effects in the suppression of superconductivity in hydrogenated Zr2Rh (Salunke, Das, Raj, Shashikala, Sathyamoorthy, Dhar; Phys. Rev. B 53, 12299)
note: Zr2H2Rh is Zr2RhH2, a hydride of the C16 superconductor Zr2Rh (Tc about 11 K). Salunke et al. (PRB 53, 12299, 1996) describe an observed suppression of superconductivity when Zr2Rh is hydrogenated. They attribute the lower Tc of Zr2RhH2 to the Fermi level moving into a valley of the density of states, and they compare with low-temperature specific-heat data. The available abstract gives no Tc for Zr2RhH2 and no lowest measured temperature, and I could not retrieve the full text or the experimental companion paper. So I cannot say whether Zr2RhH2 has a strongly reduced Tc or none above some temperature. An INIS record titled 'Superconductivity in the Zr-Rh-H(D) system', with isotope-effect and ultralow-temperature keywords, hints that some Zr-Rh-H(D) phase superconducts at low temperature, but which composition is unknown. The evidence points to Zr2RhH2 being non-superconducting or having a much lower Tc than Zr2Rh, but this is unconfirmed. The web-search budget ran out and the APS and INIS hosts were not reachable.

source_title: A structural study and some magnetic properties of Hf1-xMoxFe2 Laves phase materials (Sarr et al.)
note: HfFe2 is a Laves-phase ferromagnet, with its magnetism carried by the Fe moments. Its Curie temperature is about 600 K for x = 0 in the Hf1-xMoxFe2 study, and Mo or Al substitution lowers TC (Hf(Fe1-xAlx)2 reaches TC = 0 near x = 0.6). No superconductivity is reported. The 600 K value comes from a search-result abstract snippet; the publisher page could not be fetched to confirm the full citation and year.

source_title: Nonstoichiometric A15-Type Phases in the Systems Cr-Pt and Cr-Os (Waterstrat and van Reuth) - phase identification only
note: Cr15Pt4 is Cr0.79Pt0.21. That is exactly where the off-stoichiometric Cr-Pt A15 phase ('Cr3Pt', Cr3Si type, a about 4.71 A) is reported: 21 +/- 1 at.% Pt after 1 week at 1200 C (Waterstrat and van Reuth, AIME Trans., 1960s). I found no resistivity, susceptibility or specific-heat data for this phase and no statement of a Tc or of absence of superconductivity. Matthias et al. (Phys. Rev. 128, 588, 1962) studied Cr-Ru, Cr-Rh and Cr-Ir but not Cr-Pt. Related Cr-based A15 compounds: Cr3Ru superconducts at about 3.3 K, an A15 Cr-Ir alloy with 85 at.% Cr at about 0.77 K, and Cr3Si is non-superconducting. I have a vague memory that old A15 surveys list Cr3Pt as non-superconducting above about 1 K, but I could not verify it and did not use it. The web-search budget ran out and several hosts (Springer, onemine) were not reachable.

I found no report of a YPd4B phase under any spelling (YPd4B, Pd4YB, YBPd4). The nearest work is on the Y-Pd-B-C system. Cava et al. (Nature 1994) found 23 K superconductivity in multiphase YPd5B3C0.3, but that comes from a metastable borocarbide that needs carbon and rapid quenching. A Physica C study says carbon-free as-cast YPd3B2 shows no superconductivity down to 4.2 K. The alkaline-earth analogues SrPd4B and BaPd4B (Z. Anorg. Allg. Chem. 2010) are described as diamagnetic metals, and the snippet I saw mentions no superconductivity. None of these is the stoichiometric YPd4B, so I give no verdict on superconductivity.

source_title: Tuning of the Electronic and Vibrational Properties of Transition Metal Selenides TSe2 (T = Os, Ru) and Their Metallization at High Pressures (Naumov et al., JETP Letters 111, 456-462)
note: At ambient pressure RuSe2 is a pyrite-type semiconductor. Transport gives an indirect gap of about 1.5 eV (arXiv:1604.01755, Enhanced thermoelectric power and electronic correlations in RuSe2), and no ambient-pressure superconductivity is reported. Under pressure it becomes a metal by about 15 GPa, then a superconductor. The maximum Tc is about 5.5 K near 40 GPa, and Tc stays roughly flat above 35 GPa. Transport was measured down to 1.8 K and up to 43 GPa. Raman spectra show the pyrite structure kept up to the highest pressure. Superconductivity is therefore reported only under pressure. I could not open the full text because the host is blocked from this session, so the figures come from the abstract and the Russian summary returned by search.
second_reader_reason: I confirmed the ambient-pressure ground state by opening the arXiv paper (abstract and full text). Pyrite RuSe2 is a semiconductor with a transport gap of about 1.5 eV, measured down to 2 K with no superconductivity. Ambient superconductivity is clearly ruled out. The first pass's pressure-only claim (Naumov et al., JETP Lett. 111, 456 (2020), DOI 10.1134/S0021364020080044: metallization by about 15 GPa, Tc up to about 5.5 K near 40 GPa, data down to 1.8 K) is what put it in superconductor_only_pressure_doping_or_film. I could not open that paper: link.springer.com does not resolve from this session, the web-search budget was used up, and I know of no arXiv version. The first pass itself took the figures from a search-result abstract, not the paper. On the evidence I could verify, the verdict is semiconductor with no superconductivity at ambient pressure. If the Naumov et al. pressure result is confirmed, the verdict becomes superconductor_only_pressure_doping_or_film with Tc about 5.5 K at about 40 GPa. Neither reading makes RuSe2 an ambient-pressure superconductor.

source_title: Reversible Tuning of the Heavy-Fermion Ground State in CeCoIn5 (Pham, Park, Maquilon, Thompson, Fisk; Phys. Rev. Lett. 97, 056404; arXiv:cond-mat/0611655)
note: Ce4Co4In17Cd3 has Ce:Co:(In+Cd) = 1:1:5, so it is the nominal 15% Cd-doped heavy-fermion compound CeCo(In0.85Cd0.15)5 (CeCoIn4.25Cd0.75). The undoped parent CeCoIn5 superconducts at 2.3 K. Pham et al. (PRL 2006) show that Cd doping drives it smoothly to an antiferromagnetic ground state, and that pressure on the x = 0.10 and 0.15 samples reverses this, following the pressure behaviour of CeRhIn5 (antiferromagnetic at ambient, superconducting under pressure). A neutron study of nominal 10% Cd gives TN = 3 K with Tc = 1.3 K. NMR (Urbano et al., PRL 2007) shows the x = 0.10 and x = 0.15 samples have the same internal field. From memory, and not confirmed in what I could reach: the nominal x = 0.15 sample orders antiferromagnetically near 3 K and has no bulk superconductivity at ambient pressure, with superconductivity returning under pressure. I also recall, unverified, that the real Cd content is only about one tenth of nominal, about 1.5% of In sites, far below the 10.7 at% Cd in the formula. The exact TN, the lowest temperature measured and the pressure-induced Tc for x = 0.15 are not confirmed, because the search budget ran out and arXiv and APS pages could not be fetched from this session. If x = 0.15 in fact shows ambient coexistence of antiferromagnetism and superconductivity, the verdict would change to superconductor_ambient.
second_reader_reason: I opened the full arXiv version of Pham et al., PRL 97, 056404 (2006) and read its figures. Ce4Co4In17Cd3 is the nominal composition CeCo(In0.85Cd0.15)5. In the paper's specific-heat phase diagram (Fig. 2a), x=0.15 is purely antiferromagnetic at ambient pressure, with TN about 3.8 K read from the figure. That is higher than the 'near 3 K' the first pass recalled; about 3 K is the x=0.10 value. Under 0.95 GPa, x=0.15 becomes a bulk superconductor: Fig. 3(c) shows zero resistance at about 2.2 K, read from the figure, and ac susceptibility confirms it is bulk. tc_k=2.2 is that under-pressure value. Caveats against a cleaner verdict: (1) Fig. 3(c) also shows the 0 GPa resistivity of x=0.15 dropping to zero near about 0.9-1 K, and Fig. 3(a) plots Tc of about 0.5 K for x=0.15 at ambient pressure. The text, however, classifies x>0.12 as 'only antiferromagnetism' from heat capacity and notes that the resistive Tc runs above the thermodynamic Tc in these alloys. So bulk ambient superconductivity is not established, but filamentary or minority superconductivity below 1 K at ambient cannot be excluded. (2) The paper confirms the first pass's recollection that real Cd content is about 10% of nominal (about 1.5% of In sites, about 1.1 at% Cd overall). The written formula (10.7 at% Cd) therefore matches only the nominal label. The crystals actually measured are far more than 2 at% from it, and the composition as written has probably never been made.

note: I found no experimental or computational report on Ti2MoGa (Ti50Mo25Ga25) as a Heusler compound or as an alloy. The only Ti-Mo-Ga experiment found is a superelastic bcc Ti-7Mo-4Ga (at%) alloy, a very different composition, with no low-temperature data. I could run only one search for this compound before the shared search budget ran out, so a second spelling (for example MoTi2Ga or Ti-Mo-Ga superconductivity) was not tried.

Alloy Zr0.75V0.25. I found no readable source. The WebSearch budget was used up before my first query, doi.org and journals.aps.org do not resolve, and I know no arXiv ID for a Zr-V study. Alloy Mo0.5W0.5, part of the continuous bcc Mo-W solid solution, nonmagnetic. I found no readable source. Fe and Bi are essentially immiscible, and the only binary Fe-Bi compound I recall is FeBi2, made at high pressure (Walsh et al., ACS Cent. Sci. 2016, recalled, not verified). By valence counting, any phase of this composition would be a wide-gap band insulator, like La2O3 and SrO, and could not be a metal or superconductor. I could not confirm that this phase has been made in bulk. The CaFe2O4-type SrLn2O4 family is known for the smaller rare earths (Gd to Lu, Y), and I found no paper for La. I also found no transport or susceptibility source. The WebSearch budget was used up before my first query, doi.org and journals.aps.org do not resolve, and only arxiv.org is reachable. Alloy Ti0.80Zr0.20. No literature search was possible because the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was used up and external reference sites cannot be reached. source_title: Mossbauer measurements in iron-base alloys with nontransition elements (I. Vincze and A. T. Aldred, Phys. Rev. B 9, 3845)
note: Fe0.95Sn0.05 is an iron-rich bcc (alpha-Fe) solid solution. Sn dissolves in alpha-Fe up to several at.% at high temperature.
